sections.title: Hello, Gopherlings
sections.blurb: Say hello and learn how gopherlings works.

sections.title: Basic Types
sections.blurb: Ints, floats, bools, and honest conversions.

sections.title: Control Flow
sections.blurb: if, for, switch, and the occasional label.

sections.title: Structs & Methods
sections.blurb: Your own types, with behavior attached.

sections.title: Standard Library
sections.blurb: Batteries included: time, json, io, testing.

exercises.name: Hello, Gopher
exercises.blurb: Fix your first compile error.
hints: Go is case-sensitive: `Message` and `message` are two different names. The variable declared in greeting is called `message`.
The compiler error says `undefined: Message` and points at the exact line. Return the `message` variable instead.

exercises.name: Formatting with fmt
exercises.blurb: Build strings with fmt.Sprintf and the %s verb.
hints: `fmt.Sprintf` works like `fmt.Printf` but returns the string instead of printing it: `fmt.Sprintf("Welcome to gopherlings, %s!", name)`.
The %s verb is replaced by the string argument. Make sure the exclamation mark is there: "Welcome to gopherlings, %s!"

exercises.name: Your First Line
exercises.blurb: Write the body of your first function.
hints: The `+` operator adds two numbers: `a + b`.
Replace `return 0` with `return a + b`.

exercises.name: Declaring Variables
exercises.blurb: Fix declarations whose types do not match their values.
hints: Read the compiler errors: each one tells you the type of the value and the type you declared.
The declared type must match the value: 5 is an int, true is a bool, 3.14 is a float64.
Change the types, not the values: `var count int`, `var ready bool`, `var pi float64`.

exercises.name: Zero Values
exercises.blurb: See what uninitialized variables hold in Go.
hints: Declare the three variables with `var` and nothing after the name: `var n int`.
Do not assign anything -- Go fills in each type's zero value for you.
The body becomes: `var n int`, `var s string`, `var b bool`, then `return n, s, b`.

exercises.name: Multiple Assignment
exercises.blurb: Swap two variables in one statement.
hints: One statement can assign several variables: `x, y = y, x`.
The right-hand side is evaluated before anything is assigned, so no temporary variable is needed.
Write `a, b = b, a` before the return.

exercises.name: Constants
exercises.blurb: Declare constants correctly and learn why they cannot change.
hints: Constants use `=`, never `:=`: `const days = 7`.
A constant cannot be reassigned -- the `days = 8` line must go.
daysInWeek should just be `return days`.

exercises.name: Enumerations with iota
exercises.blurb: Number the weekdays automatically with iota.
hints: In a const block, `iota` starts at 0 and counts up by one on every line.
Give the first line `Sunday = iota` and leave the other lines with no value at all -- they repeat it.
The block is `Sunday = iota` followed by Monday through Saturday on their own lines, and isWeekend returns `d == Saturday || d == Sunday`.

exercises.name: Integer Division
exercises.blurb: Watch int / int throw away the remainder.
hints: When both operands are ints, `/` truncates: 3 / 2 is 1, not 1.5.
float64(a + b) converts the sum BEFORE the division; the current code converts after, when it is too late.
Return `float64(a+b) / 2`.

exercises.name: Floating Point
exercises.blurb: Compare floats with an epsilon, not ==.
hints: 0.1 + 0.2 is not exactly 0.3 in binary floating point -- it differs by about 5e-17.
Call the values equal when their absolute difference is below a tiny threshold: math.Abs(a-b) < 1e-9.
Replace the body of nearlyEqual with exactly that comparison.

exercises.name: Booleans & Comparisons
exercises.blurb: Combine comparisons with && and ||.
hints: Inclusive means the boundaries count: x may be equal to lo or to hi.
Two conditions are needed: x >= lo AND x <= hi, joined with &&.
Return `x >= lo && x <= hi`.

exercises.name: Numbers & Strings
exercises.blurb: Convert between strings and numbers with strconv.
hints: A string is not a number: `s * 2` cannot compile. Import strconv and parse with strconv.Atoi.
strconv.Atoi returns two values: `n, _ := strconv.Atoi(s)`. Ignoring the error with _ is fine for now.
The body is `n, _ := strconv.Atoi(s)` followed by `return strconv.Itoa(n * 2)`.

exercises.name: Multiple Return Values
exercises.blurb: Return two values at once and receive them with `q, r :=`.
hints: Go returns several values as a comma-separated list: `return q, r`.
The quotient is `a / b` and the remainder is `a % b`.
The whole fix is one line: `return a / b, a % b`.

exercises.name: Named Return Values
exercises.blurb: Name your return values and let a naked return send them home.
hints: The naked `return` sends back whatever the named results hold right now.
`rest` was never assigned, so it still holds its zero value, 0.
Add `rest = sum - half` before the `return`.

exercises.name: Variadic Functions
exercises.blurb: Write a function that accepts any number of int arguments.
hints: Inside the function, `nums` is just a []int slice — range over it.
Start the largest value at the first element (`nums[0]`), not at 0, so all-negative input works too.
Loop with `for _, n := range nums`; whenever `n > largest`, set `largest = n`. Return `largest` at the end.

exercises.name: Closures
exercises.blurb: Return a function that remembers its own private counter.
hints: The returned function can use variables declared in `counter` — that is what makes it a closure.
Declare `count := 0` in `counter`, before the `return func() ...` line.
Inside the returned function: `count++` and then `return count`.

exercises.name: if and else
exercises.blurb: Route an int through if, else if and else to one of three answers.
hints: You need three outcomes, so you need all three parts: `if`, `else if`, `else`.
The zero case comes last: when x is neither positive nor negative, it must be 0.
`if x > 0 { return "positive" } else if x < 0 { return "negative" } else { return "zero" }`.

exercises.name: Loops with for
exercises.blurb: Go has one loop keyword: write the classic and the while-style for.
hints: Both functions need a variable that changes as the loop runs — declare it before the loop.
sumTo: `for i := 1; i <= n; i++ { total += i }`. powerOfTwo: keep doubling while `exp > 0`.
powerOfTwo body: `result *= 2` and `exp--` each round; return `result` afterwards.

exercises.name: switch
exercises.blurb: Replace an if/else chain with a tagless switch for letter grades.
hints: In a tagless switch every case is a full condition, like `case score >= 90:`.
Order matters — the first matching case wins, so the highest range goes first.
Add `case score >= 90: return "A"`, then 80 -> "B", 70 -> "C", 60 -> "D", above the default.

exercises.name: Labels, break & continue
exercises.blurb: Break out of nested loops with a label and find the first negative.
hints: A plain `break` only leaves the inner loop; the outer one happily keeps scanning.
Put a label before the outer `for` (like `outer:`), then `break outer` to leave both loops.
Declare `first := 0` before the loops; when you find a negative, store it and `break outer`. Return `first` after the loops.

exercises.name: FizzBuzz
exercises.blurb: The classic capstone: loops, conditionals and a slice you build with append.
hints: You need one string per number, appended in loop order: `result = append(result, s)`.
Check "divisible by both 3 and 5" FIRST — otherwise "Fizz" would catch 15 before FizzBuzz gets a chance.
If/else chain: `i%3 == 0 && i%5 == 0` -> "FizzBuzz", `i%3 == 0` -> "Fizz", `i%5 == 0` -> "Buzz", else `strconv.Itoa(i)`.

exercises.name: Struct Literals
exercises.blurb: Create structs with keyed literals and compare their fields.
hints: The compiler error `too few values in Point literal` is about the unkeyed literal Point{3}: it must list every field in order, and one is missing.
Switch to the keyed form: Point{X: 3, Y: 4}. Keyed literals keep working when fields are reordered or added.
samePoint compares field by field: `return a.X == b.X && a.Y == b.Y`.

exercises.name: Methods
exercises.blurb: Give Rect an Area method with a value receiver.
hints: Inside a method, the receiver (r) is the value the method was called on: r.W and r.H are its fields.
The area of a rectangle is width times height.
Replace the TODO line with `return r.W * r.H`.

exercises.name: Pointer Receivers
exercises.blurb: Fix a method that silently edits a copy of its receiver.
hints: Scale compiles but changes nothing: a value receiver hands the method a copy, and the copy is thrown away when the method returns.
Change the receiver in Scale's signature from Rect to *Rect so the method can reach the caller's rectangle.
`func (r *Rect) Scale(f float64)` -- field writes like r.W *= f then land in the original; Go auto-dereferences, so no extra * is needed.

exercises.name: Embedding
exercises.blurb: Use an embedded struct's promoted field in a method.
hints: Because Engine is embedded in Car (no field name), Engine's fields are promoted: a Car can read Horsepower as c.Horsepower.
Describe is one fmt.Sprintf call: %s for the make, %d for the horsepower.
`return fmt.Sprintf("%s with %d HP", c.Make, c.Horsepower)` -- exact wording matters: "Zephyr with 210 HP".

exercises.name: Slice Fundamentals
exercises.blurb: Index into a slice and sum it up with range.
hints: Indexing starts at 0, so the second element lives at xs[1].
For total, declare sum := 0 before the loop, then walk the slice with `for _, v := range xs`.
Add each value to the sum inside the loop (`sum += v`) and return it after the loop.

exercises.name: Growing with append
exercises.blurb: Grow a slice with append, and keep the slice it returns.
hints: append(xs, v) returns the grown slice -- but growing may allocate a new backing array, so the result can be a different slice value than xs.
Keep the return value: the idiomatic line is xs = append(xs, v).
push can be a one-liner: `return append(xs, v)`.

exercises.name: Slice Aliasing
exercises.blurb: Copy a slice so the original stops sharing its memory.
hints: Returning xs directly hands back the very memory the test's orig uses -- the test writes res[0] = 99 and watches orig change with it.
You need a fresh backing array with the elements copied over. The slices package has a helper for exactly this.
`return slices.Clone(xs)` -- or the classic `append([]int(nil), xs...)`.

exercises.name: Slice Expressions
exercises.blurb: Cut a slice down to its middle with a slice expression.
hints: You want the elements from index 1 up to -- but not including -- index len(xs)-1: one slice expression, no copying.
Handle the short cases first: if len(xs) < 3 there is no middle, so return nil.
`return xs[1 : len(xs)-1]` -- the range is half-open: index 1 is in, index len(xs)-1 is out. Like cloneOf showed, it shares memory with xs.

exercises.name: 2D Slices
exercises.blurb: Build an identity matrix as a slice of slices.
hints: Start with `grid := make([][]int, n)`: n rows, each still nil and waiting for its own make.
Loop over the rows, and for each row allocate the columns: `grid[i] = make([]int, n)`.
Inside a nested loop over the columns, put a 1 where the row index equals the column index: `if i == j { grid[i][j] = 1 }`.

exercises.name: Map Literals
exercises.blurb: Create a map with a literal and meet the zero value missing keys return.
hints: A nil map is not the same as an empty map: you have to create one, either with a literal or with make.
A map literal writes the type followed by the pairs: map[string]int{"alice": 31, ...}.
Make ages return map[string]int{"alice": 31, "bob": 27}.

exercises.name: The comma-ok idiom
exercises.blurb: Tell a missing key apart from a stored zero value.
hints: m[k] on a missing key just returns 0, so it cannot tell you whether the key was there at all.
The comma-ok idiom asks for the value and an existence flag in one go: v, ok := m[k].
Replace the return with `v, ok := m[k]` on one line and `return v, ok` on the next.

exercises.name: Deleting Keys
exercises.blurb: Remove an entry from a map with the delete builtin.
hints: Go ships a builtin for exactly this: delete(m, key).
delete(m, k) mutates m in place. Maps are reference types, so returning m afterwards is enough.
The whole body is two lines: delete(m, k), then return m.

exercises.name: Iterating Maps
exercises.blurb: Range over a map and collect its keys in sorted order.
hints: for k := range m visits every key, but in randomized order, so sort before returning.
Collect the keys into a []string inside the loop, then sort the slice with sort.Strings.
keys := make([]string, 0, len(m)); fill it with append in the loop; sort.Strings(keys); return keys. The modern one-liner is slices.Sorted(maps.Keys(m)).

exercises.name: len Counts Bytes
exercises.blurb: Count characters, not bytes, with utf8.RuneCountInString.
hints: len(s) counts bytes, and some characters take more than one byte in UTF-8.
utf8.RuneCountInString(s) counts runes: the characters you actually see.
return utf8.RuneCountInString(s). Counting the steps of a `for range s` loop works too.

exercises.name: Reversing Runes
exercises.blurb: Reverse characters, not bytes, so multi-byte letters survive.
hints: The swap loop is fine, it is just operating on bytes, which shreds two-byte letters.
Convert to []rune first so each element is a whole character, then convert back with string().
r := []rune(s); keep the loop but swap r[i] and r[j]; return string(r).

exercises.name: The strings Package
exercises.blurb: Trim, lowercase and replace spaces using strings helpers.
hints: The strings package has ready-made helpers. You need three of them, chained.
strings.TrimSpace trims the edges, strings.ToLower lowercases, strings.ReplaceAll(s, " ", "-") swaps spaces for hyphens.
return strings.ReplaceAll(strings.ToLower(strings.TrimSpace(s)), " ", "-")

exercises.name: strings.Builder
exercises.blurb: Join lines efficiently with strings.Builder instead of +.
hints: Every s += x copies the whole string; strings.Builder appends into one buffer instead.
Declare var b strings.Builder, WriteString each piece, then return b.String() at the end.
Loop over the lines; write "\n" before every line except the first, then return b.String().

exercises.name: Taking & Dereferencing
exercises.blurb: Take an address with &, follow it with *, and double the value behind a pointer.
hints: `p` holds an address; the value lives behind it. `&x` takes an address, `*p` follows one.
Go has no pointer arithmetic -- the only thing to do with p here is dereference it before multiplying.
Replace the body with `*p *= 2`.

exercises.name: Nil Pointers
exercises.blurb: A nil pointer points at nothing -- check it before you follow it.
hints: The zero value of a pointer is nil, and dereferencing nil panics at runtime.
Compare the pointer against nil first and return the zero string from that branch.
Start the function with `if p == nil { return "" }`, then `return *p`.

exercises.name: Swap via Pointers
exercises.blurb: Pass pointers so a function can really exchange its caller's two variables.
hints: The call sites pass `&x` and `&y`, but the parameters are plain ints -- the types do not match.
Change the signature to `func swap(a, b *int)`, then combine multiple assignment with dereferencing.
The body becomes a single line: `*a, *b = *b, *a`.

exercises.name: Implicit Satisfaction
exercises.blurb: Make Dog satisfy Speaker by giving it the method the interface asks for.
hints: There is no `implements` keyword: a type satisfies an interface just by having its methods.
Speaker wants a method named Speak returning string. Dog already has the right shape under the wrong name.
Rename Dog's Bark method to Speak, and make announce return "It says: " + s.Speak().

exercises.name: Programming to Interfaces
exercises.blurb: Loop over a []Speaker and collect what each one says.
hints: One interface, many types: the slice holds Dogs, Cats and Robots, but you only ever call Speak().
Start with an empty []string, range over the speakers, and append each s.Speak().
`said := make([]string, 0, len(speakers))`, then `said = append(said, s.Speak())` inside `for _, s := range speakers`.

exercises.name: Type Switches
exercises.blurb: Use a type switch to name the kind of value hiding inside an any.
hints: A type switch looks like a regular switch, but each case names a type: `switch v.(type) { case int: ... }`.
Cover int, string, bool and nil, then default for the rest. Bind a variable (switch x := v.(type)) only if you use it -- an unused binding is a compile error.
`case nil:` catches v == nil and returns "nothing"; default returns "unknown".

exercises.name: The Stringer Interface
exercises.blurb: Add one method so fmt prints your type the way you want.
hints: At print time fmt checks whether a value has a String() string method, and calls it for %v.
Give Temperature a method with receiver `(t Temperature)`; convert to float64 before formatting.
`func (t Temperature) String() string { return fmt.Sprintf("%.1f°C", float64(t)) }`

exercises.name: Method Sets Gotcha
exercises.blurb: Pointer-receiver methods live only on *T -- store the pointer in the interface.
hints: Inc has a pointer receiver, so it belongs to *Counter's method set, not Counter's.
The fix is at the marked assignment: hand the interface a *Counter instead of a Counter value.
`var inc Incrementer = &c` -- now the interface holds a pointer whose method set has both methods.

exercises.name: Returning Errors
exercises.blurb: Return an error value next to the result instead of dividing by zero quietly.
hints: Go has no exceptions here: problems come back as an error value beside the result, nil when all is well.
Guard the function with `if b == 0` and build the error with errors.New (you will need to add the "errors" import).
Return `0, errors.New("cannot divide by zero")` in that branch, and `a / b, nil` otherwise.

exercises.name: Sentinel Errors
exercises.blurb: Return the one shared ErrNotFound value so errors.Is can recognize it.
hints: errors.Is compares error VALUES, not their text -- the current code mints a new error on every call.
The ErrNotFound sentinel is already declared at the top of the file; use it.
Replace `errors.New("not found")` inside find with `ErrNotFound`.

exercises.name: Wrapping Errors
exercises.blurb: Wrap ErrNotFound with the key as context, keeping the error chain intact.
hints: %v formats the wrapped error into the message but drops the link to it -- the text looks right and errors.Is fails.
fmt.Errorf has a wrapping verb, %w, which embeds the error AND records it for errors.Is to find.
Change %v to %w in the fmt.Errorf call: `fmt.Errorf("load %q: %w", key, ErrNotFound)`.

exercises.name: Custom Error Types
exercises.blurb: Return a typed error carrying the field name, and let errors.As dig it out.
hints: Any type with an Error() string method is an error -- ValidationError already qualifies.
errors.As stores the concrete *ValidationError into its second argument when the chain holds one; a plain fmt.Errorf hides the field forever.
Return `&ValidationError{Field: "age"}` when age is negative.

exercises.name: Type Parameters
exercises.blurb: Replace two type-specific Max functions with one generic Max.
hints: A generic function declares type parameters in square brackets right after its name: func Max[T cmp.Ordered](a, b T) T.
Import "cmp": cmp.Ordered is a ready-made constraint covering every type that supports < -- all the numbers plus strings.
Max's body is exactly MaxInt's body. Delete MaxInt and MaxFloat, then let the test infer T for ints, floats, and strings.

exercises.name: Writing Constraints
exercises.blurb: Make a union-constrained sum actually add up its slice.
hints: The signature is already right; the body never touches xs, so total stays at zero.
Range over xs and accumulate each element into total inside the loop.
for _, x := range xs { total += x }, then return total after the loop.

exercises.name: The comparable Constraint
exercises.blurb: Search any slice of comparable values for the first match.
hints: indexOf always returns -1 -- it never looks at xs.
Range with the index: for i, x := range xs, and return i the first time x == v.
If the loop finishes without a match, return -1.

exercises.name: Generic Types
exercises.blurb: Generalize IntStack into a Stack that stores any element type.
hints: Rename IntStack to Stack[T any] and swap every int in the struct and its methods for T.
Methods restate the type parameter in their receiver: func (s *Stack[T]) Push(v T).
For Pop on an empty stack, var zero T is the zero value of whatever T turns out to be.

exercises.name: Channels
exercises.blurb: Pass a value through a channel, then signal that it is closed.
hints: A send is ch <- n; it hands the value over to a receiver.
close(ch) tells receivers that no more values will arrive.
The whole body: ch <- n, then close(ch).

exercises.name: go Statements
exercises.blurb: Run the sends on a goroutine so they can meet their receiver.
hints: The test does not start receiving until fillAsync has returned, so an inline send on the unbuffered channel blocks with nobody to receive it.
Wrap the send loop in go func() { ... }() so fillAsync can return while the sends continue in the background.
Inside the goroutine: defer close(ch), then loop over nums sending each value.

exercises.name: select
exercises.blurb: Merge two channels into one with a select loop.
hints: select with one case per input receives from whichever channel has a value ready.
Receive as v, ok := <-a: ok == false means that channel is closed and drained. Setting the variable to nil disables its case.
Loop while a != nil || b != nil; when both are nil, fall out and let defer close(out) run.

exercises.name: WaitGroups
exercises.blurb: Sum a slice in parallel chunks with goroutines and a WaitGroup.
hints: Split nums into `parts` contiguous chunks and give each chunk to its own goroutine.
Call wg.Add(1) before each go, defer wg.Done() inside, and wg.Wait() after the loop; each goroutine sends its partial sum on a shared (buffered) channel.
After wg.Wait(), close the channel and range over it, adding the partial sums into the total.

exercises.name: sync.Mutex
exercises.blurb: Guard a shared map against 200 concurrent writers with a mutex.
hints: Add a mu sync.Mutex field to SafeCounter; its zero value is ready to use.
Lock at the top of Increment before writing the map, and in Get before reading it.
Make defer mu.Unlock() the line right after each Lock.

exercises.name: context
exercises.blurb: Let a blocking wait bail out early when the context is cancelled.
hints: Waiting only on <-ready never looks at ctx, so a cancelled context is ignored.
select on both channels: <-ready means return nil; <-ctx.Done() means return ctx.Err().
ctx.Err() is context.Canceled for a cancelled context -- exactly what the test checks with errors.Is.

exercises.name: Time & Durations
exercises.blurb: Turn a number of seconds into a compact duration string.
hints: A time.Duration counts nanoseconds, and time.Second is one too — so time.Duration(s) * time.Second is the duration for s seconds.
Put the duration in a variable and call its String method: `d := time.Duration(s) * time.Second; return d.String()`.
One-liner: `return (time.Duration(s) * time.Second).String()` — 90 becomes "1m30s", 3661 becomes "1h1m1s".

exercises.name: encoding/json
exercises.blurb: Marshal a struct to JSON, with the tags deciding the keys.
hints: You will need to add the "encoding/json" import; json.Marshal(u) returns ([]byte, error).
Check the error first — return "" if err != nil — otherwise convert the bytes with string(data).
`data, err := json.Marshal(u); if err != nil { return "" }; return string(data)`.

exercises.name: io.Reader
exercises.blurb: Drain an io.Reader, count the bytes, and pass errors along.
hints: io.ReadAll(r) reads until EOF and returns the bytes plus an error; len(data) is the byte count.
Do not swallow the error: if err != nil, return it unchanged so the caller can react.
`data, err := io.ReadAll(r); if err != nil { return 0, err }; return len(data), nil`.

exercises.name: defer & recover
exercises.blurb: Catch a panic with defer and recover instead of crashing.
hints: A deferred function runs when catchPanic exits — even while a panic is unwinding through it.
Inside the deferred closure, `if recover() != nil` means f panicked; assign true to the named return `panicked`.
`defer func() { if recover() != nil { panicked = true } }()` placed before the call to f().

exercises.name: Write Your Own Test
exercises.blurb: The code is correct this time — you write the table-driven test.
hints: A table-driven test declares a slice of structs with inputs and wanted results, then loops over it with t.Errorf on mismatches.
Shape: `cases := []struct{ in string; want bool }{...}`, then `for _, c := range cases { if got := isPalindrome(c.in); got != c.want { t.Errorf(...) } }`.
Make sure the table includes "Level" -> false (case-sensitive!) and "" -> true, plus the other cases listed in exercise.go.
